To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
age-related declines in word recognition are associated with gray matter changes in left auditory cortex (HG) and with activity in the dorsal portion of the ACC.

the left HG/STGs of younger and older adults differ in gray matter volume, which predicts word recognition performance, and that this relationship is mediated by error-monitoring activity in the dorsal cingulate cortex.
the ability of younger and older adults to recognize speech is dependent on a left HG/STC region and that the integrity of this region is associated with error monitoring activity in dorsal ACC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of age-related differences in speech processing.
the neurobiology of speech perception, with a focus on the auditory and language systems.
the relationship between age-related changes in the brain, hearing and cognition, and how these changes impact speech recognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
speech perception is a highly complex process that is dependent upon a variety of factors.
speech perception in older adults is affected by both peripheral and central factors, which are not necessarily related to hearing loss, but are likely related to the aging brain.
older adults exhibit a deficit in speech recognition, and this is related to a structural change in a region of cortex involved in processing speech.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

age-related differences in word recognition can be partially explained by structural differences in the left HG/ST G, and that this relationship is reflected by differences in error monitoring in the ACC.
the ability to recognize and understand speech is dependent on low-level auditory cortex, and that this ability is compromised in older adults.
older adults have a more difficult time with speech recognition than younger adults and that the difficulty is related to structural differences in the brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ability to recognize words in noise depends on the morphology of the low-level auditory cortex.
the auditory system is not a simple system, but one that is highly integrated with other brain regions.
age-related declines in speech recognition are associated with structural changes in auditory cortex and attentional systems.
